New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a new policy today that will ban younger schoolchildren from using AI in classrooms. The one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, will impact about 600,000 public school students in 2-K through eighth grade and is being introduced alongside additional limits on digital devices and a small pilot program for AI education tools.

The new rules being introduced by NYC’s Department of Education will bar teachers from using AI tools to grade assignments, and keep students from using the technology in the classroom until they enter high school, with chatbots designed specifically for companionship and mental support reportedly being banned in all grades. High school aged students will only be permitted to use AI in specific instances, and they’ll be offered AI literacy classes twice a year to help students “think critically” before they come to “rely on it.”

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” Mamdani said in a statement. “The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way.”

Use of individual screens will be banned until third grade. The department is also issuing recommended screen time limitations, which include a maximum of 45 minutes per day for middle schoolers. Teachers will still be permitted to use AI for lesson planning, and exceptions may be granted for AI tools that help students with disabilities or multilingual students. Exceptions can also be granted for particular purposes like computer science programs.

A “limited AI pilot” program will also be offered at up to five classes in a “small number” of high school classrooms, using tools that were vetted to meet safety and data privacy standards, and “keeping students as the primary thinker.” Tools being piloted by this program have set time limits for usage, and include Quill for English language support, Edia for math, Brisk Teaching for guiding study practice, and Playlab and Intel AI-Ready Schools for multi-subject support.

These changes follow NYC’s public school system introducing a bell-to-bell ban on “personal internet-enabled electronic devices” (including smartphones) for the 2025-2026 school year. NYC district leaders say the new AI moratorium for classrooms is one of the most restrictive policies in the US, though some countries like Norway , Sweden , and the Netherlands have implemented nationwide changes to address similar concerns about the impact that technology is having on developing minds.

overhaul By Phil Taitt Wednesday, September 2, 2026 4:25PM Brian Shlonsky has the details from Fort Greene, Brooklyn. NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other city officials announced a sweeping new policy Wednesday imposing a one-year ban on student use of generative artificial intelligence in New York City public schools from 2-K through 8th grade, while limiting screen time for younger students and launching AI literacy lessons for high schoolers.

The moratorium, which takes effect during the 2026-27 school year, will affect nearly 600,000 students, roughly two-thirds of the city's public school enrollment.

"This moratorium is a commitment to getting the future right," Mamdani said. "We will embrace new technology, but only when it serves our students."

City officials said student-facing AI tools and companion chatbots will be prohibited for younger grades while a coalition of educators, parents, experts and elected officials studies the technology's impact and recommends next steps.

A limited number of high school classrooms will be allowed to participate in closely monitored AI pilot programs, and all high school students will receive twice-yearly lessons focused on AI literacy, bias, ethics and critical thinking.

Officials said teachers will still be permitted to use AI for lesson planning and administrative work that meets city safety standards.

The policy also introduces new screen time guidelines, including restrictions on one-to-one device use for the youngest students and recommended daily caps of 30 minutes for grades 3-5 and 45
reactions: [Hacker News] Keeping younger students away from computers is dumb, but we do need to go back to the basic computer literacy classes of the early/mid 2000s, e.g. typing, basics of desktop operating systems like the filesystem, using word, powerpoint etc. It's appalling how lacking high schoolers seem to be in these kinds of skills.

[Hacker News] In highschool, students learn to use many tools which are physically dangerous, including automobiles, stovetops, carpentry and metal fabrication tools, chemical laboratory equiment, and may even compete in archery or rifle events. All of these things can be used for good or for harm, and we introduce them when students are a little older. Why can't AI be on this list?

[Hacker News] Even if you're pro-AI, there's a reason calculators are banned from math classes until a certain point. It seems like a no-brainer to have people learn on hammers before moving them to nailguns. I can't help but think of this Chesterton Quote: "It is, on the contrary, a thing analogous to writing one's own love-letters or blowing one's own nose. These things we want a
[Hacker News] Was this written by AI? What is a load-bearing statement?
[Hacker News] Sure, if the kids want to learn. But let’s be honest, most of them, or even us, are just going to use the chatbot directly for the answer.

[Hacker News] probably for the best. just like how calculators are banned in classrooms until you get the hang of computation, AI should be banned while critical thinking/writing/social skills are still being developed
[Hacker News] Yep, just like the tech elite. Peter Thiel limits his kids to 90 min/week screentime.
[Hacker News] This is a load-bearing statement, students will get left behind. Chinese students getting distilled knowledge will lead to a performance gap that New York students may never overcome.

[Hacker News] Communicating with adults and handling the friction of conversing with others is a skill students need to gain, especially at this age. Talking to a machine that will always suit your style of talking isn't always good.
[Hacker News] It's not a good idea. The students will get left behind.
[Hacker News] Makes sense. I had to learn how to add / subtract before I could use a calculator. Note: This policy doesn't seem to apply to high school

[Hacker News] They'll need to keep on top of this, or one day it'll look like banning 'word processors' in schools. Seems like a similar path would be sensible: at first it's a topic for IT, but over time it'll creep into all subjects.
